title: On the Incarnation
hook: Athanasius, at about twenty-five, explains why the Word became flesh

segments.voice: Yesterday, Origen's search: scripture as body, soul and spirit, read as a climb. Your line was read upward. Where did your verse take you? Day one thousand two hundred forty.

A great king enters a great city and moves into one house on one street. Just one. And yet, the story goes, the whole city is honored. Robbers who had been circling it lose their nerve, because the king lives there now. Nobody dares treat that city as a soft target anymore. That small parable comes from a short book by Athanasius, who became bishop of Alexandria. The book asks a question at the center of the Christian story: why would God's Word become a human being? Its title is today's word: On the Incarnation.

Athanasius starts with a problem. People were made in God's image, made from nothing and held in being by God. But turning from God, they were sliding back toward nothing: toward death and decay. And God, he says, couldn't simply watch his own work fall apart. That would be unworthy of God. So what could be done? Here he gives a second picture. A portrait painted on wood has been ruined, smeared until the face is gone. The painter doesn't throw away the board. The person in the portrait comes back and sits again, so the likeness can be redrawn on the same wood. That, for Athanasius, is the Incarnation. The Word of God came and took a body like ours, so the image could be restored from inside humanity, and death undone by his rising. Paul has a line for the coming down: Christ "took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men." Now the king in the city makes sense. By living in one human body, the Word honored every human body, and the powers that preyed on us lost their grip. Near the end of the book, Athanasius says it in one breath, here in paraphrase: he became human so that we might be made divine. Orthodox Christians call that sharing theosis. Catholics and some Protestants speak of it in the words of Second Peter: "partakers of the divine nature." Churches describe it differently. Athanasius's starting point is plain enough: God didn't stay far away.
screen: `A PORTRAIT REDRAWN ON THE SAME WOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a line of it, and let it sit. Settle, and breathe. Here is Athanasius's picture, in paraphrase: the person in the portrait comes back and sits again, so the likeness can be redrawn on the same wood. Say it slowly in your head. Then notice what it says about the wood. Not thrown away. Kept. Worked on. Think of one thing in your own life that feels smeared or ruined. Let the picture sit beside it, without forcing anything. If you pray, you can offer it to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
On the Incarnation. Athanasius's short book on why the Word of God became human: to restore God's image in us from the inside, like a king who moves into the city.
Your line: a king in the city. Today, when you walk down an ordinary street, remember the picture: one house, and the whole city honored. Day one thousand two hundred forty.

howItsDone: Christians confess in the Nicene Creed that the Son of God was incarnate and made man; churches celebrate the Incarnation at Christmas and the Annunciation.

fork.setup: you're a painter. a portrait on wood has been smeared until the face is gone. what do you do?
options: throw away the board and start over.
have the person sit again and redraw the face on the same wood.
fork.reveal: that's Athanasius's picture of the Incarnation: the Word comes in person, so God's image can be restored in the same humanity, not replaced.

notes: Index hook says 'at about twenty-five'; the age is cut under the claims rule (dating of On the Incarnation is debated). Script says only 'a churchman of Alexandria who later became its bishop'. Confirm.

All Athanasius material is paraphrased (no public-domain translation quoted): the king in the city (ch. 9), the slide toward non-being and God's 'unworthy' to let it perish (4–6), the portrait on wood (14), 'he became man that we might be made God' (54). Confirm chapter numbers and wording.

Theosis: 'Orthodox Christians call that sharing theosis; Catholics and some Protestants speak of it in the words of Second Peter' (softened to 'some Protestants'). Keeper to decide on fairness across churches.
'Short book' describes On the Incarnation; confirm acceptable.

Editor pass: 'a young teacher' cut to 'a churchman of Alexandria' (age claim; Athanasius's role when writing is debated). 'All of them start where Athanasius did' (sweeping claim about all churches) replaced.

Audit pass: "a churchman of Alexandria who later became its bishop" took a side in the debated dating of On the Incarnation (before or after 328); now "who became bishop of Alexandria".
